introduction_markdown:

Answer ALL the SIX questions in this booklet. The mark allocation is indicated for each question. Each question carries 20 marks. In calculations you are advised to show all the steps in your working, giving your answer at each stage. All necessary working must be shown. No marks will be awarded for answers without brief statements showing how the answers have been obtained. Calculators may be used.

**Useful data:** one atmosphere (1 atm) = 1 Pa = $1.01\times10^{5}$ N m$^{-2}$ (as printed); relative atomic masses (RAM): C = 12.0, S = 32.0, O = 16.0, H = 1.0; molar gas volume at stp = 22400 cm$^3$.

questions.enonce_markdown:
An organic compound X contains 54.9% carbon, 10.9% hydrogen and 13.9% nitrogen. A molecular weight determination of the compound gave a value of 230. (R.A.M: C = 12, N = 14, H = 1, O = 16)

(i) Calculate the empirical formula of the compound.

(ii) Determine the molecular formula of the compound.

(iii) Suggest the structural formula for compound X given that it gives butylamine when warmed with bromine and concentrated potassium hydroxide. *[5 marks]*

(iv) How can you test for the presence of nitrogen in the compound X? *[3 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Empirical formula.** The percentages add up to $54.9 + 10.9 + 13.9 = 79.7\ \%$; since an RAM for oxygen is supplied, the remaining $100 - 79.7 = 20.3\ \%$ is taken to be oxygen.

| Element | % by mass | % / RAM | Ratio (divide by smallest, 0.993) |
|---|---|---|---|
| C | 54.9 | 4.575 | 4.61 |
| H | 10.9 | 10.9 | 10.98 |
| N | 13.9 | 0.993 | 1.00 |
| O | 20.3 | 1.269 | 1.28 |

The ratio C : H : N : O = 4.6 : 11 : 1 : 1.3 cannot be turned into whole numbers by any small multiplier (x2 gives 9.2 : 22 : 2 : 2.6, x4 gives 18.4 : 44 : 4 : 5.1...), and a molar mass of 230 would require $0.139 \times 230 / 14 = 2.3$ nitrogen atoms. **The numerical data printed in the question are therefore not mutually consistent.** Part (iii) fixes the compound: Hofmann degradation to butylamine, $\mathrm{C_4H_9NH_2}$, shows that X is the amide with one more carbon, pentanamide. Pentanamide, $\mathrm{C_5H_{11}NO}$, has $M = 5(12) + 11(1) + 14 + 16 = 101$, and its composition is H 10.9 % and N 13.9 % (exactly the printed values), C 59.4 % and O 15.8 % (the printed 54.9 % for carbon seems to be a misprint).

Working from the H and N data: $\mathrm{H : N} = 10.9 : 0.993 = 11 : 1$, with $\mathrm{C : N} \approx 5 : 1$.

**Empirical formula: $\mathrm{C_5H_{11}NO}$.**

**(ii) Molecular formula.** Empirical formula mass $= 101$. $n = \dfrac{M_r}{101}$. The printed $M_r = 230$ gives $n = 2.28$, which is not a whole number, so it cannot be right; the formula consistent with part (iii) has $n = 1$ ($M_r = 101$). **Molecular formula: $\mathrm{C_5H_{11}NO}$** (the printed value 230 is not usable).

**(iii) Structure.** Heating an amide with bromine and concentrated KOH is the **Hofmann degradation**: $\mathrm{R{-}CONH_2} \rightarrow \mathrm{R{-}NH_2}$, the product having **one carbon fewer**. Butylamine ($\mathrm{C_4H_9NH_2}$) therefore comes from an amide with 5 carbons:

$$\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2CH_2CONH_2}$$

X is **pentanamide**. $\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2CH_2CONH_2} + \mathrm{Br_2} + 4\mathrm{KOH} \rightarrow \mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2CH_2NH_2} + \mathrm{K_2CO_3} + 2\mathrm{KBr} + 2\mathrm{H_2O}$

**(iv) Test for nitrogen.** *Lassaigne sodium fusion test:* fuse a small sample with a piece of sodium metal in an ignition tube, heat strongly until red hot, and plunge the tube into distilled water. Boil and filter: the filtrate (sodium fusion extract) contains sodium cyanide, formed from the carbon and nitrogen of the compound. Add freshly prepared iron(II) sulphate solution, boil, then add a little iron(III) chloride and acidify with dilute sulphuric (or hydrochloric) acid: a **Prussian blue** colour or precipitate shows that nitrogen is present: $3\mathrm{[Fe(CN)_6]^{4-}} + 4\mathrm{Fe^{3+}} \rightarrow \mathrm{Fe_4[Fe(CN)_6]_3}$

(For an amide, a simpler confirmation: boil with aqueous NaOH; ammonia is evolved and turns damp red litmus paper blue.)

questions.enonce_markdown:
An organic compound with molecular formula $\mathrm{C_4H_9O_2N}$ has both the amino and carboxylic acid functional groups and is optically active.

(i) What is a functional group?

(ii) Give the condition for a compound to be optically active

(iii) Give the optical isomers of the compound. *[4 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** A functional group is an **atom or group of atoms in a molecule that is responsible for its characteristic chemical reactions** (e.g. the amino group $-\mathrm{NH_2}$ and the carboxylic acid group $-\mathrm{COOH}$).

**(ii)** A compound is optically active (it rotates the plane of plane-polarised light) when its molecules are **chiral**: not superimposable on their mirror image. This needs, normally, an **asymmetric (chiral) carbon atom** bonded to **four different atoms or groups**, and no plane or centre of symmetry.

**(iii)** The compound is **2-aminobutanoic acid** (an alpha-amino acid), $\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH(NH_2)COOH}$. Carbon 2 is bonded to four different groups: $-\mathrm{H}$, $-\mathrm{NH_2}$, $-\mathrm{COOH}$ and $-\mathrm{CH_2CH_3}$. It exists as a pair of **enantiomers**, mirror images of each other (Fischer projections):

```
         COOH                     COOH
          |                        |
  H2N --- C --- H          H --- C --- NH2
          |                        |
         CH2CH3                   CH2CH3
  L-(S)-2-aminobutanoic    D-(R)-2-aminobutanoic
         acid                     acid
```

The two forms rotate the plane of polarised light by equal amounts in opposite directions; an equimolar mixture (racemic mixture) is optically inactive.

questions.enonce_markdown:
1,2-dimethylbromoethane $(\mathrm{CH_3})_3\mathrm{CBr}$ reacts with aqueous NaOH under reflux.

(i) Give the equation for the reaction.

(ii) What type of mechanism is illustrated by the reaction? Write out the mechanism. *[5 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
(The compound $(\mathrm{CH_3})_3\mathrm{CBr}$ is 2-bromo-2-methylpropane, a tertiary halogenoalkane.)

**(i)** $\mathrm{(CH_3)_3CBr} + \mathrm{NaOH} \rightarrow \mathrm{(CH_3)_3COH} + \mathrm{NaBr}$  (or, ionically, $(\mathrm{CH_3})_3\mathrm{CBr} + \mathrm{OH^-} \rightarrow (\mathrm{CH_3})_3\mathrm{COH} + \mathrm{Br^-}$). The organic product is 2-methylpropan-2-ol.

**(ii) Type of mechanism: nucleophilic substitution, unimolecular ($S_N1$).**

*Step 1 (slow, rate-determining):* heterolytic fission of the polar C-Br bond (the bonding pair goes to bromine) gives a tertiary carbocation and a bromide ion:

$\mathrm{(CH_3)_3CBr} \rightarrow \mathrm{(CH_3)_3C^{+}} + \mathrm{Br^{-}}$

*Step 2 (fast):* the hydroxide ion, a nucleophile, uses a lone pair on oxygen to attack the positive, planar carbon (curly arrow from the lone pair of $\mathrm{OH^-}$ to carbon):

$\mathrm{(CH_3)_3C^{+}} + \mathrm{OH^{-}} \rightarrow \mathrm{(CH_3)_3COH}$

Why $S_N1$: the tertiary carbocation is stabilised by the electron-releasing (positive inductive) effect of the three methyl groups, and the bulky methyl groups hinder a back-side attack that $S_N2$ would need. The rate depends only on the halogenoalkane: $\text{rate} = k[(\mathrm{CH_3})_3\mathrm{CBr}]$ (first order).

questions.enonce_markdown:
Give the product(s) of the following reactions of Phenylethanone with (1) NaOH / $\mathrm{I_2}$, (2) 2,4-DNPH and (3) HCN(g).

![fig-1](gce-al-chemistry-2023-p2-officiel-cameroun_exercice_5_fig_1.png)

2,4-DNPH is 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine, $\mathrm{H_2NNH{-}C_6H_3(NO_2)_2}$ (structure shown in the figure). *[3 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
Phenylethanone (acetophenone), $\mathrm{C_6H_5COCH_3}$, is a methyl ketone.

1. **NaOH / $\mathrm{I_2}$** (iodoform test): the methyl ketone is oxidatively cleaved to the carboxylate salt and a yellow precipitate forms. Products: **sodium benzoate**, $\mathrm{C_6H_5COONa}$, and **triiodomethane (iodoform), $\mathrm{CHI_3}$**, a pale yellow solid: $\mathrm{C_6H_5COCH_3} + 3\mathrm{I_2} + 4\mathrm{NaOH} \rightarrow \mathrm{C_6H_5COONa} + \mathrm{CHI_3} + 3\mathrm{NaI} + 3\mathrm{H_2O}$

2. **2,4-DNPH** (condensation, nucleophilic addition-elimination at C=O): an orange-yellow precipitate of the **2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazone**, $\mathrm{C_6H_5C(CH_3){=}NNHC_6H_3(NO_2)_2}$, with loss of water: $\mathrm{C_6H_5COCH_3} + \mathrm{C_6H_3(NO_2)_2NHNH_2} \rightarrow \mathrm{C_6H_5C(CH_3){=}NNHC_6H_3(NO_2)_2} + \mathrm{H_2O}$

3. **HCN** (nucleophilic addition of cyanide to the carbonyl group, in the presence of a little base or cyanide ion as catalyst): the **cyanohydrin 2-hydroxy-2-phenylpropanenitrile**, $\mathrm{C_6H_5C(OH)(CH_3)CN}$: $\mathrm{C_6H_5COCH_3} + \mathrm{HCN} \rightarrow \mathrm{C_6H_5C(OH)(CH_3)CN}$
